preamble: Assimilation of the coda tap [ɾ] to a following voiceless stop, giving a voiceless [t]: a geminate [tt] or [t˺t] before /t/, and [t˺tʃ] before /tʃ/. In western Cuban Spanish (the provinces from Pinar del Río to Matanzas and Cienfuegos, including Havana, plus the municipalities of Corralillo and Trinidad), coda /ɾ/ and coda /l/ merge and assimilate to the next consonant. Lamb (1968) describes a voiceless onset before tense [pp], [tt] and [kk] as a variant of r in Havana; Goodgall de Pruna (1970) reports the same in Trinidad, Ruiz Hernández (1974) in Pinar del Río, Havana and Matanzas, and Guitart (1978, 2004) describes [t˺t] and [t˺ʧ]. Choy López (1984) records voiceless and voiced results as free variants (dificu[tt]oso ~ dificu[dt]oso). This is a competing description of the sequence filed under ɾ > d: Costa Sánchez (1984), the acoustic study of Ruiz Hernández and Miyares Bermúdez (1984) and Carlson (2017) found the first element voiced (all as summarized by Arias 2019). Arias (2019) writes these sequences as Guitart transcribes them across word boundaries, but notes that the realization is the same within words, where he writes [d˺t] and [d˺ʧ]; the transcriptions differ only because they follow different descriptions, not because the pronunciations differ. The unassimilated pronunciations remain more common.
